messages.subject: nqrank interpretation question
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I recently did an analysis where I ran scanone() followed by stepwise() and fitqtl() using unadjusted phenotype data and then again using the nqrank transformation to evaluate them using the normal quantiles of the ranks as many of the phenotypes I'm working with are non-normal (sometimes dramatically... p=10^-15 in a shapiro-wilk test).

I had a couple questions on how I might think about the interpreations:

1) There were several phenotypes where the QTL results were different (not surprisingly). Though sometimes the transformed phenotypes detected more QTL than the unadjusted ones. I would expect spurious signal detection in the non-normal data, but was somewhat surprised to see additional QTL showing up when the same phenotype was transformed. Given the only difference between the analyses is the transformation, is it reasonable to assume the differences are due to violations of normality in the unadjusted data and that the nqrank() results are more believable?

> 1a) Also, in a few cases the unadjusted phenotypes were normal already and I transformed them to see how the results would change anyway, and they did change. Would it be recommended that I only transform the phenotypes that violate normality egregiously? But leave the others untransformed as the analysis itself is somewhat robust to some departure from normality?

2) How do I interpret the estimated effects of a phenotype that's been transformed in this way? For example, if the estimated effect of the QTL is -0.2, that reflects that the allele at that locus reduces the normal quantile of the rank by 0.2? Or the phenotypic value itself by 0.2 compared to the alternate allele?

Both results look reasonable in terms of the LOD scores, number of QTL detected etc..., though there are more biological consistencies using the nqrank results (i.e. phenotypes I would expect to be under similar genetic control showing similar QTL results to each other).

I should mention that I'm working with a RIL SSD rice population. Thresholds were determined by 1000 permutations. I'm confident in the quality of both the phenotype data and the genotype data (30k SNPs). Not sure what other details would be relevant.

Any thoughts would be helpful. Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] nqrank interpretation question
messages.body_plain:
The issues with transforming phenotypes for QTL analysis are the same as for transforming the outcome in multiple linear regression.

The estimated effects are hard to interpret following transformation.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] nqrank interpretation question
messages.body_plain:
If a permutation test is used to define thresholds, the transformation shouldn't affect the false positive rate. The hope is to improve power.

But if the original phenotype is approximately normally distributed, the transformation shouldn't do much, and so it's strange that the results would be markedly different. I would try to figure out why.

karl

messages.body_plain:
I got the following email and thought it and my response might be useful to others.

> I performed composite interval mapping (CIM) analysis using R/QTL.
>
> I found a QTL detected at position 7.14 cM at the LOD value of 6.95 on one of the chromosome.
>
> When I calculate confidence interval using LOD drop and Bayesian, I get very wide interval (4.55-85.04cM).
>
> If I look at the plot, it shows two QTL peaks. However, the second one remains undetected in CIM analysis. I have attached QTL plot for your reference.
>
>
> Do you have any suggestions?
>
> I used following command:
> gsl <- calc.genoprob(gsl,step=2.0,off.end=0.0,error.prob=1.0e-4,map.function="kosambi",stepwidth="fixed")
> out.cim<-cim(gsl,pheno.col=13,n.marcovar=5,map.function="kosambi",error.prob=1.0e-4,window=10,method="hk")
> summary(out.cim,threshold=3)
> A03_16278726 A03 42.83 7.71
> B3_8339813   A08 35.68 3.39
> A09_2046302  A09  7.14 6.93
>
> CIchrA09<-lodint(out.cim,chr="A09",drop=1.8)
> CIchrA09
>            chr   pos      lod
> A09_1376566  A09  4.55 4.224291
> A09_2046302  A09  7.14 6.930171
> A09_35937880 A09 85.04 4.912760

lodint() only works well when there is one QTL on the chromosome. In your case, I suggest subsetting to have it consider only the positions <40 cM or >40 cM:

lodint(out.cim[out.cim[,2]<40,], chr="A09", drop=1.8)

lodint(out.cim[out.cim[,2]>40,], chr="A09", drop=1.8)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

I am kinda confused with how to deal with interactions in QTLs. I tried the following to determine which pairs of QTLs are interacting and I got several significant interactions based on the p-values.

addint(data, qtl=qtl, method="hk")

When I looked at the plot from plotLodProfile, it appears that there is an additional QTL on the same chromosome based on the same 0.05% LOD cutoff (I think that is not real).

Is it right to fit interactions into the model that way, or is there a different way to deal with interactions?

Let me know if you need more information or clarity.

Thanks,
CJ

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Interactions in QTLs
messages.body_plain:
The profile LOD curves when you have an interaction in the model will also include the interaction term: comparing q1+q2+q1:q2 and q2 alone, or q1+q2+q1:q2 and q1 alone. The threshold to consider is not just the main effect threshold.

To see whether there's evidence for an additional QTL on a chromosome, use addqtl().

karl

messages.body_plain:
Depending on the QTL positions, the results of addqtl will change, as they are conditional on the locations of the initial QTL.

It's hard to say what's going on with refineqtl without a bit more information. The function performs a scan for the location of  each QTL, one at a time, keeping other QTL at fixed positions, seeking to improve the likelihood. It's not guaranteed to find the global optimum.

The best you can do is estimate a genetic map and then get average rates for each chromosome, as genetic length / physical length.
